title: Types of variables
summary: Continuous, discrete, nominal, ordinal: the type decides which summaries and charts make sense.

steps.title: Kinds of variable
body: Before computing anything, ask what *kind* of values a column holds:
| **Continuous** numeric | height, price, temperature | mean, median, std, any arithmetic |
| **Discrete** numeric | number of children, items in basket | counts, mean, median |
| **Nominal** categorical | country, colour, product | counts, mode, share |
| **Ordinal** categorical | t-shirt size S/M/L, rating 1–5 stars | order, median, counts |
Plus **dates/times**, **free text** and **identifiers** (order id, zip code), which are labels even when they look like numbers.
The kind decides the summary (averaging countries is nonsense), the chart (a histogram for continuous, bars for categories)
and how a model must encode it.

steps.prompt: What kind of variable is it?
items: Number of items in an order
Education level: school / bachelor / master / PhD

steps.prompt: A `zip_code` column holds values like `2134` and `90210`. What kind of variable is it?
options: Nominal categorical: it is a label that happens to use digits
steps.explain: The average zip code means nothing, and 90210 is not 'more' than 2134. Treat it as text (and keep leading zeros).

steps.title: The right summary for the kind
body: For ordinal data you need the **order**, which the values alone do not carry: sorted alphabetically, `L < M < S < XL`.
pandas expresses these kinds as dtypes: `int64`/`float64` numbers, `str` text, `bool`, `datetime64` dates and

steps.explain: pandas infers a dtype per column. Each kind gets the summary that suits it: a mean for prices, a mode for countries (ties resolve alphabetically).
